facts_checked_2026_11_25.frame_time: 1000 ms / rate: 60 -> 16.67 ms, 120 -> 8.33 ms, 144 -> 6.94 ms ('under seven'); 60->120 saves 8.33 ms, 120->144 saves 1.39 ms ('under one and a half')
facts_checked_2026_11_25.ltpo: LTPO OLED backplanes (LTPS + oxide TFTs) vary refresh from 120 Hz down to 1 Hz for static content / always-on display (Android Authority, Digital Trends, How-To Geek); base iPhone 17 ships 1-120 Hz ProMotion (Engadget, PhoneArena, Sep 2025) - generic in the script
facts_checked_2026_11_25.gaming_phones: RedMagic 11S Pro 144 Hz, claims 3,000 Hz touch sampling (TechRadar, Jun 2026); ROG Phone 9 Pro 165 Hz (GSMArena) -> '144 or 165 hertz', 'thousands of times a second'
facts_checked_2026_11_25.monitors: ZOWIE XL2586X+ rated 600 Hz (BenQ/ZOWIE product page, 2026; PC Gamer, RTINGS lists) -> 'esports monitors now hit 600'; unverified 1,100 Hz claim not used
facts_checked_2026_11_25.tearing_vrr: tearing = buffer swap during scan-out when frame rate and refresh are not in sync; G-Sync / FreeSync (VRR) make the display refresh when each frame is ready, within its range
facts_checked_2026_11_25.pixels: active-matrix panels redraw line by line; each pixel's TFT circuit with a storage capacitor holds its drive level until the next refresh (sample-and-hold)
facts_checked_2026_11_25.platform_note: YouTube and Instagram play at most 60 fps, so 120/144 are shown slowed down (said in S05)

scenes.text: Your screen isn't playing a video. It's flipping still pictures. 60, 120, even 144 every second.
scenes.visual: Hook world 'Flipbook': a premium smartphone full-bleed, tilted in 3D, already moving on frame 0; on 'flipping' its screen lifts off and fans out into a stack of glowing frame cards that riffle like a flipbook (each card the same neon ball a step further along); a big counter lands 60 -> 120 -> 144 on the numbers.

scenes.text: Two numbers decide how smooth it feels. Frames per second: how fast your chip draws pictures. Hertz: how often your screen refreshes.
scenes.visual: World 'Two machines': a graphics chip as a frame factory printing frame cards onto a glowing conveyor (gauge 'FPS'), feeding a screen drawn as a window with a refresh shutter that blinks (gauge 'Hz'); 'Frames' lights the factory, 'Hertz' lights the screen.

scenes.text: At 60, each picture gets 16.7 milliseconds. At 120, just 8.3. At 144, under seven.
scenes.visual: World 'Time lanes': three glowing lanes labelled 60, 120, 144 Hz; in each a light bar sized to one frame's time (16.7 ms, 8.3 ms, 6.9 ms) with a stopwatch ring sweeping; each lane's bar snaps to its size on its number.

scenes.text: Every refresh, the screen redraws itself row by row. Inside each pixel, tiny transistors hold its color until the next refresh.
scenes.visual: One continuous NanoZoom into the screen: phone screen -> display stack (cover glass, touch layer, OLED) -> pixel grid with a bright scan line redrawing row by row -> one pixel (red, green, blue subpixels) -> its tiny transistor and storage capacitor glowing as they hold the color until the scan line passes again.

scenes.text: This video only plays at 60, so let's slow time down. At 60 hertz, a moving ball jumps in big steps. At 120, the steps are half as big, so motion looks smoother.
scenes.visual: World 'Slow time': a clock face slows inside time-warp rings ('slowed 8x' tag); a ball arcs along two tracks leaving ghost dots where each refresh shows it: the 60 Hz track has a few big gaps, the 120 Hz track twice as many dots; on 'smoother' the 120 track's trail turns into one fluid line.

scenes.text: But fast refresh drains battery, so phones cheat. LTPO screens shift speed on the fly: up to 120 when you scroll, slower when you read, just 1 hertz on the lock screen.
scenes.visual: World 'Gearbox phone': a phone with a refresh dial / gear lever beside it; it shifts 120 (a fast-scrolling feed) -> lower (an article being read) -> 1 Hz (always-on lock-screen clock), and a battery gauge drains slower with each shift down. Generic phone, no brand.

scenes.text: Gaming phones push to 144 or 165 hertz, with touch sensors checking your finger thousands of times a second.
scenes.visual: World 'Touch grid': a gaming phone in landscape with shoulder-trigger glow; a fingertip on the glass, the capacitive grid beneath it pulsing rings outward; badges 144 Hz and 165 Hz; a touch-scan counter rolls into the thousands per second.

scenes.text: On a PC, the graphics card must keep up. Say it makes 90 frames for a 144 hertz monitor. The screen catches half of one frame and half of the next. That's tearing.
scenes.visual: World 'Tear': a PC graphics card printing frames at 90 per second beside a 144 Hz monitor whose scan line sweeps faster; out of step, a game scene (neon spaceship over a city) splits along a horizontal tear line where the new frame starts mid-scan; the tear is highlighted on 'tearing'.

scenes.text: The fix is variable refresh, like G-Sync or FreeSync. The monitor waits for each new frame, and refreshes the moment it lands.
scenes.visual: World 'Sync': the same monitor and card; the scan line now waits at a gate; each frame card lands, a green sync light flashes and the scan runs; G-Sync and FreeSync shown as two labelled badges; the spaceship scene glides with no tear.

scenes.text: And each jump gives less. 60 to 120 saves 8 milliseconds a frame. 120 to 144, under one and a half. Yet esports monitors now hit 600.
scenes.visual: Light act 'Diminishing stairs': an evidence card with two steps - '60 -> 120: -8.3 ms per frame' (a big step) and '120 -> 144: -1.4 ms' (a tiny step) with a marker sweep; footnote 'frame time = 1000 / Hz'; on '600' a sleek esports monitor badge '600 Hz' rises at the top.

scenes.text: So, frames per second is how fast pictures are made. Hertz is how fast they're shown. Smooth is when they match.
scenes.visual: Callback to the hook: the FPS gauge and the Hz gauge swing to the same number and lock together with a click; the flipbook from the hook now plays perfectly smooth on the phone.

scenes.text: Follow for part two: what input lag really is.
scenes.visual: Phone CTA: fingertip presses Follow, it flips to Following; a small 'Part 2: Input lag' card slides up; hold the last frame.
